shots.narration: Eleven places on Earth can kill anyone who stays.
We ranked them, roughly, by how fast.
Doug has a suitcase and a ticket to all eleven.
Doug did not agree to this.
Hours.
Death Valley.
This long, dry basin in California holds the official world record for the hottest air ever measured.
On July tenth, nineteen thirteen, a thermometer here read one hundred and thirty-four degrees Fahrenheit, about fifty-seven Celsius.
A study in two thousand twenty-five argued that the reading was a mistake and that the real high was closer to one hundred and twenty,
but for now the record still stands. Either way, a normal July afternoon here averages about one hundred and sixteen.
Doug arrives in flip-flops with one small bottle of water, and he says the place is nice.
Here's the problem. Doug is watching the wrong thermometer.
On July fifteenth, nineteen seventy-two, the ground at Furnace Creek reached two hundred and one degrees Fahrenheit,
only eleven degrees short of the point where water boils.
The air that same afternoon was one hundred and twenty-eight,
so the ground was seventy-three degrees hotter than the air above it.
The real heater in Death Valley is the floor, which soaks up sunlight all day and gives it back from below.
Night is not much of a break.
On summer nights, the temperature may only drop to between eighty-five and ninety-five degrees,
so the valley never gets a real chance to cool off.
Your body cools itself by sweating, and sweat is made of water.
Doug's entire water supply is one small bottle, and it is empty before lunch.
Doug decides to sit down for a minute, right on the ground,
which we have just established is the hottest thing in the valley.
The most famous number in Death Valley might be wrong,
but the ground has never needed a record to win.
Snake Island.
Thirty-three kilometers off the coast of Brazil sits a small, forested island called Queimada Grande,
and almost nobody is allowed to visit it.
Its most famous resident is the golden lancehead,
a pit viper that lives nowhere else on Earth.
The entire wild population is on this one island, the species is critically endangered,
and landing is restricted to the Brazilian navy and authorized scientists.
As an adult, the golden lancehead mostly eats birds,
and it relies heavily on two species that stop on the island in certain seasons.
Researchers have found that its venom is more potent in birds than in mammals,
which makes sense for a snake whose dinner can fly away.
The strange part is that the famous number is fake.
You may have heard that the island has one snake for every square meter.
It doesn't. The first real population estimate, published in two thousand eight, came to about two thousand three hundred snakes,
and more recent estimates put it between two and four thousand.
The island covers forty-three hectares, about the size of sixty soccer fields,
which gives each snake a bit less than a tennis court of forest.
That is still a lot of snakes, but they aren't standing shoulder to shoulder.
Doug crouches down, holds out a hand and tries to make friends,
because he has decided the snake looks lonely. It has a few thousand neighbors.
On the island's only trail, the rate at which researchers met snakes
fell by about half between the nineteen nineties and the two thousands,
and they found signs of illegal collecting.
The island is closed to visitors, and these days that rule protects the snakes as much as the people.
Morecambe Bay.
On the northwest coast of England, the tide goes out twice a day
and leaves about three hundred and ten square kilometers of sand and mud behind.
It looks like the biggest, flattest beach in the country,
and on a sunny day it looks completely harmless.
People have crossed these sands on foot for a very long time,
and the bay even has an official King's Guide to the Sands, a local expert who leads walkers across.
The local museum service lists the most common causes of accidents out here:
quicksand, fog, and the speed of the incoming tide.
Quicksand is a mix of fine sand, clay and salt water,
and if you stand still, it can feel almost solid.
Start wriggling, and it suddenly behaves like a liquid, so you sink.
Then the sand around your legs settles to the bottom and packs tight,
like wet concrete that has decided to keep you.
Here's the twist. Quicksand cannot actually swallow you.
In two thousand five, physicists at the University of Amsterdam tested it in the lab.
The average human body is about half as dense as quicksand,
so a person sinks to about the waist and then floats,
and nobody vanishes with one hand waving.
Getting out is another story.
According to the same team, pulling one leg free takes about the same force as lifting a small car.
Doug is stuck to the waist, and he is very relaxed about it,
because he watched a video that said quicksand can't pull him under.
He is completely right.
Then the tide arrives.
Quicksand doesn't need to pull anyone under,
because it only has to keep them in place until the sea gets there.
Lake Natron.
In northern Tanzania, near the border with Kenya,
there's a shallow lake with a reputation online for turning any animal that touches it into stone.
The water is loaded with dissolved sodium carbonate, which makes it strongly alkaline.
On the scale chemists use, it measures between nine and ten and a half,
not far from household ammonia at about eleven.
In places, the water can also reach sixty degrees Celsius,
while a hot tub is never supposed to go above forty.
For most animals, this is a place to avoid. For one bird, it's home.
About three quarters of the world's lesser flamingos are born here.
The adults have tough, leathery skin on their legs, so the water doesn't bother them much,
and they build their nests on islands of salt crust.
The caustic water around those islands works like a moat that predators can't cross.
But that's not the disturbing part.
The preserved animals are real, but the poses aren't.
The famous photos come from the photographer Nick Brandt and were published in two thousand thirteen.
He found birds and bats that had died and washed up along the shore,
already preserved by the salts in the water,
and in his own words, he then placed them in living positions.
The lake preserves bodies, but it doesn't arrange them.
Doug is here in a lesser flamingo costume, to blend in,
and he stands on one leg like a professional.
The flamingos ignore him, and the lake leaves him alone.
He survives. We'll be honest, this was not the plan.
A lake this caustic is also the main nursery of the lesser flamingo.
Minutes.
Antarctic Plateau.
In the middle of East Antarctica, the ice sheet rises into a high, flat plateau
more than three and a half kilometers above sea level.
This is where Earth keeps its coldest air.
On July twenty-first, nineteen eighty-three, Vostok Station recorded
minus eighty-nine point two degrees Celsius,
which is still the official record for the coldest air ever measured on the ground.
For scale, a home freezer is set to about minus eighteen,
so your kitchen is about forty degrees warmer than your freezer.
Vostok was about seventy degrees colder than it.
However, Vostok was not even the coldest spot.
Here's the worst part. Satellites mapped the snow surface along a high ridge between two ice domes,
Dome Argus and Dome Fuji, and in winter, small hollows there reached about minus ninety-eight degrees Celsius.
The recipe is clear skies and extremely dry air,
which let the snow's heat escape straight into space.
The cold, heavy air then slides into the hollows, gets trapped and keeps cooling.
The National Weather Service has a chart for how fast bare skin freezes,
and it only goes down to about minus forty-three Celsius.
At the coldest corner of that chart, the answer is five minutes.
Even the air in these hollows, at around minus ninety-four,
is more than fifty degrees colder than the bottom of the chart.
Doug has brought sunscreen, because the last few places were sunny.
It is the middle of the polar winter, and the sun has not come up in weeks.
The coldest spots on Earth were found by satellite,
because there was no thermometer standing in them.
Everest Death Zone.
The summit of Mount Everest is eight thousand eight hundred and forty-nine meters above sea level,
about the height of twenty-three Empire State Buildings stacked on top of each other.
Above about eight thousand meters, climbers call it the death zone.
The air up here has the same mix of gases as at the beach, there's just much less of it.
At the summit, the air pressure is about a third of what it is at sea level,
so every breath brings in roughly a third of the oxygen.
People do stand here, but they get here slowly, over a long climb that gives the body time to adjust.
Researchers who measured climbers on Everest found that their blood carried more and more of the oxygen-carrying protein on the way up,
and many climbers also breathe bottled oxygen.
Even then, scientists describe the summit as close to the limit of what a human can tolerate.
Doug skipped all of that and was delivered straight to the top.
Here's the problem. Pilots have a number for this, called the time of useful consciousness,
which is how long a person has to act sensibly once the oxygen runs short.
According to the Federal Aviation Administration's table, at the height of Everest's summit,
that time is somewhere between one and three minutes.
After that, nobody gets to decide anything.
Doug plants a tiny flag with his own name on it,
then takes a moment to admire the view.
The view is incredible, and it is also most of his remaining minutes.
On the highest point on Earth, the view is perfect,
and each breath is a third of one.
Cave of Crystals.
About three hundred meters down a mine in northern Mexico,
miners broke into a chamber filled with crystals so big they look fake,
and it may be the most beautiful room on Earth.
The crystals are gypsum, and the biggest ones are about eleven meters long,
about the length of a city bus.
They grew slowly in hot, mineral-rich water, sealed underground, over an enormous stretch of time.
The cave only had air in it because the mine's pumps kept the water out,
and what the water left behind was the heat.
The air in the crystal chambers sits around fifty degrees Celsius or more,
and the humidity is around ninety percent or higher.
That second number is the real killer.
Your body sheds heat by evaporating sweat off your skin,
but when the air is already that full of water, sweat barely evaporates,
so the cooling system simply stops working.
The air is also hotter than you are, so it heats you up instead of cooling you down.
Here comes the bad news. You get minutes.
Unprotected visits had to be kept to about ten or fifteen minutes,
so scientists built special suits packed with ice,
and those stretched a visit to about an hour.
Doug sets a ten-minute kitchen timer,
sits down on a giant crystal and lines up the perfect photo.
The timer is optimistic.
In two thousand fifteen the mine closed, the pumps stopped, and the hot water came back,
so the crystals are underwater again and can keep growing.
The most beautiful room on Earth used to give visitors about ten minutes, and now it gives them none.
Dallol.
In the Danakil Depression of northern Ethiopia,
more than a hundred meters below sea level,
there's a field of pools colored neon yellow, green and orange.
Dallol holds the world record for the highest average yearly temperature ever measured,
about thirty-four and a half degrees Celsius, recorded in the nineteen sixties.
That is the average, including every night.
Underneath, hot water rises through thick layers of salt over a body of magma,
and it comes up as boiling brine, saturated with salt and loaded with iron.
The iron, along with sulfur and other minerals, paints the pools those impossible colors.
On the acidity scale, lemon juice is about two,
and each step down is ten times stronger.
These pools measure around zero, or even below it,
so they are more than a hundred times more acidic than lemon juice.
The springs also give off acidic gases, including carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide.
Here's the strange part. Scientists came here looking for life,
and in the worst pools, they didn't find any.
Life on Earth turns up almost anywhere there's liquid water.
But in two thousand nineteen, a French and Spanish team reported no microbial life
in the hottest, saltiest, most acidic pools, or in the magnesium-rich brine lakes next to them.
In the desert and the salty canyons around the site, life was doing fine.
Another team has reported tiny microbes in the pools, so the argument is not completely settled.
Doug has brought a magnifying glass to help the search for life.
He doesn't find any, and briefly that includes him.
On a planet where life fills almost every drop of water,
these few pools may be one of the places it can't.
Seconds.
Lake Nyos.
Lake Nyos is a deep crater lake in the hills of northwest Cameroon,
and on August twenty-first, nineteen eighty-six, it released a huge cloud of gas.
Deep below the surface, the water had been collecting carbon dioxide from magma under the lake,
and the weight of the water above kept it dissolved, like a sealed bottle of soda.
That day, the balance broke. It all came out at once.
Carbon dioxide is about one and a half times as dense as air,
so instead of drifting away, it hugs the ground and flows downhill like water poured across a table.
At least one thousand seven hundred people died, along with thousands of livestock.
The scientists who investigated found that the gas was carbon dioxide from deep in the lake, not a volcanic eruption.
The most unsettling part is that the gas kept building up again after the disaster.
Since two thousand one, pipes in the lake have been lifting deep water to the surface
so the gas escapes slowly, a little at a time.
Lake Kivu, between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo,
holds hundreds of times as much gas, even by the most cautious estimates,
and around two million people live in the region.
Doug stands on the shore at night, looking out at a lake that seems perfectly calm,
and then he lies down on the grass and does not get up.
Lake Nyos still looks like a quiet lake in the hills, with a pipe in the middle to keep it that way.
Lake Maracaibo.
Lake Maracaibo in northwestern Venezuela gets more lightning than anywhere else on Earth,
and it isn't close.
A sensor aboard a NASA satellite counted lightning flashes from orbit for sixteen years,
and in two thousand sixteen, scientists used that record to rank every lightning hotspot on the planet.
Lake Maracaibo came out on top, with more than two hundred and thirty-three flashes per square kilometer per year.
That's more than one flash a year over every soccer field.
On average, it gets thunderstorms on two hundred and ninety-seven nights a year.
The recipe is local. On most nights, winds off the mountains, the lake and the sea meet over the warm water,
push humid air up, and build storms over the same spot.
The flashes are so regular that the storms have their own name, the Catatumbo lightning.
Lightning heats the air around it to about fifty thousand degrees Fahrenheit,
which is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
The main stroke is over in a few thousandths of a second.
Doug has gone night fishing on the shore, holding a long rod up toward the most electric sky on the planet,
and he has caught nothing so far.
But here's the surprising part.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, almost ninety percent of people struck by lightning survive.
Doug is fine. His cap is smoking a little,
his hair is pointing in several new directions, and he would like to go home now.
The lake with the most lightning on Earth hit Doug with something five times hotter than the Sun,
and he is mostly annoyed.
Nyiragongo.
Nyiragongo is a volcano in the Democratic Republic of the Congo,
about twelve kilometers north of the city of Goma.
For long stretches of time, its summit crater has held something rare: a lake of liquid lava.
The summit crater is about one point two kilometers wide.
The lake inside it has stretched about two hundred and thirty meters across,
roughly two soccer fields end to end.
London's Natural History Museum calls it the world's largest continuously active lava lake.
Most lava flows move slowly enough that people can walk away from them.
Nyiragongo's lava is different. It is very low in silica,
and less silica means runnier lava, so this lava flows almost like water.
It is often called the fastest-flowing lava on Earth.
In January nineteen seventy-seven, the lava lake drained in less than an hour
through cracks on the side of the mountain.
Those flows moved at up to sixty kilometers an hour,
faster than cars are allowed to drive through most towns.
And each time the lake has drained, it has eventually filled back up.
Here's the part most people never hear about:
the lava isn't the only thing that kills around this volcano.
In the low ground around Nyiragongo and Goma, carbon dioxide seeps up through cracks in the rock,
and locals call these spots mazuku, which means evil wind.
It's the same gas as at Lake Nyos, with no lake needed.
Because it is heavier than air, it collects in hollows, usually in the lowest meter of air, and stays there.
Dead animals are the usual warning sign,
because insects, birds, goats and dogs walk in and don't walk out.
So the volcano has two ways to get you:
a glowing lake on the summit that can outrun traffic,
and an invisible puddle at the bottom of the hill.
Doug has seen marshmallows go badly before,
so this time he has brought a fire extinguisher,
and also, because he has learned nothing, a marshmallow.
He points the extinguisher at a lake of lava.
The extinguisher runs out first.
Doug's cap made it, slightly toasted,
which is more than the marshmallow can say.
Doug deaths: thirty-six.
Which deadly place should Doug visit next? Tell us in the comments.
The suitcase still has room.
